entries.content_osis: Num 5:1-4 <div eID="gen1659" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1660" type="x-p"/> Removal of Unclean Persons out of the Camp. - As Jehovah, the Holy One, dwelt in the midst of the camp of His people, those who were affected with the uncleanness of leprosy (Lev 13), of a diseased flux, or of menstruation (Lev 15:2., Num 15:19.), and those who had become unclean through touching a corpse (Num 19:11., cf. <reference osisRef="Lev.21.1">Lev 21:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lev.22.4">Lev 22:4</reference>), whether male or female, were to be removed out of the camp, that they might not defile it by their uncleanness. The command of God, to remove these persons out of the camp, was carried out at once by the nation; and even in Canaan it was so far observed, that lepers at any rate were placed in special pest-houses outside the cities (see at <reference osisRef="Lev.13.45-Lev.13.46">Lev 13:45-46</reference>).

entries.content_osis: Num 5:5-10 <div eID="gen1660" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1661" type="x-p"/> Restitution in Case of a Trespass. - No crime against the property of a neighbour was to remain without expiation in the congregation of Israel, which was encamped or dwelt around the sanctuary of Jehovah; and the wrong committed was not to remain without restitution, because such crimes involved unfaithfulness (מעל, see <reference osisRef="Lev.5.15">Lev 5:15</reference>) towards Jehovah. “<hi type="italic">If a man or a woman do one of the sins of men, to commit unfaithfulness against Jehovah, and the same soul has incurred guilt, they shall confess their sin which they have done, and</hi> (the doer) <hi type="italic">shall recompense his debt according to its sum</hi>” (בּראשׁו, as in <reference osisRef="Lev.6.5">Lev 6:5</reference>), etc. האדם מכּל־חטּאת, one of the sins occurring among men, not “a sin against a man” (<hi type="italic">Luther, Ros.,</hi> etc.). The meaning is a sin, with which a מעל was committed against Jehovah, i.e., one of the acts described in <reference osisRef="Lev.6.3-Lev.6.4">Lev 6:3-4</reference>, by which injury was done to the property of a neighbour, whereby a man brought a debt upon himself, for the wiping out of which a material restitution of the other’s property was prescribed, together with the addition of a fifth of its value, and also the presentation of a sin-offering (<reference osisRef="Lev.6.4-Lev.6.7">Lev 6:4-7</reference>). To guard against that disturbance of fellowship and peace in the congregation, which would arise from such trespasses as these, the law already given in <reference osisRef="Lev.6.1">Lev 6:1</reference> is here renewed and supplemented by the additional stipulation, that if the man who had been unjustly deprived of some of his property had no <hi type="italic">Goël</hi>, to whom restitution could be made for the debt, the compensation should be paid to Jehovah for the priests. The <hi type="italic">Goël</hi> was the nearest relative, upon whom the obligation rested to redeem a person who had fallen into slavery through poverty (<reference osisRef="Lev.25.25">Lev 25:25</reference>). The allusion to the <hi type="italic">Goël</hi> in this connection presupposes that the injured person was no longer alive. To this there are appended, in Num 5:9 and Num 5:10, the directions which are substantially connected with this, viz., that every heave-offering (<hi type="italic">Terumah</hi>, see at <reference osisRef="Lev.2.9">Lev 2:9</reference>) in the holy gifts of the children of Israel, which they presented to the priest, was to belong to him (the priest), and also all the holy gifts which were brought by different individuals. The reference is not to literal sacrifices, i.e., gifts intended for the altar, but to dedicatory offerings, first-fruits, and such like. את־קדשׁיו אישׁ, “<hi type="italic">with regard to every man’s, his holy gifts...to him</hi> (the priest) <hi type="italic">shall they be; what any man gives to the priest shall belong to him</hi>.” The second clause serves to explain and confirm the first. את: <hi type="italic">as far,</hi> with regard to, <hi type="italic">quoad</hi> (see <hi type="italic">Ewald</hi>, §277, d; <hi type="italic">Ges.</hi> §117, 2, note).

entries.content_osis: Num 5:11-31 <div eID="gen1661" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1662" type="x-p"/> Sentence of God upon Wives Suspected of Adultery. - As any suspicion cherished by a man against his wife, that she either is or has been guilty of adultery, whether well-founded or not, is sufficient to shake the marriage connection to its very roots, and to undermine, along with marriage, the foundation of the civil commonwealth, it was of the greatest importance to guard against this moral evil, which was so utterly irreconcilable with the holiness of the people of God, by appointing a process in harmony with the spirit of the theocratical law, and adapted to bring to light the guilt or innocence of any wife who had fallen into such suspicion, and at the same time to warn fickle wives against unfaithfulness. This serves to explain not only the introduction of the law respecting the <hi type="italic">jealousy-offering</hi> in this place, but also the general importance of the subject, and the reason for its being so elaborately described.
